A1.justification: Both PDFs describe TableDART. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support matching retained content against additions and revisions.

before.justification: v1 reports original TableDART accuracy and BLEU results across seven benchmarks, routing ablations, inference measurements, and analyses in the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds a Qwen2.5-VL backbone variant and efficiency measurements across resource-loss weights. Its disclosure that many baseline scores come from prior publications does not alter this assessment.

M1.justification: The three inference paths, frozen experts, lightweight MLP gate, KL-plus-resource objective, and Fusion agent are retained. Expanded descriptions of binary targets and deterministic routing clarify the existing procedure. The Qwen2.5-VL variant instantiates the same framework with another visual backbone.

E1.justification: Both versions use WTQ, TABMWP, TAT-QA, HiTab, FeTaQA, TabFact, and InfoTabs for the same question-answering and fact-verification tasks. The five-dataset training mixture and exclusion of HiTab and FeTaQA from training are unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds reported comparisons against TabPedia-7B, SynTab-LLaVA-7B, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B. Existing main-table comparators and the Random Routing and Non-Adaptive Fusion ablation baselines remain.

E3.justification: Table 5 changes its aggregate from averaging all seven scores, including FeTaQA BLEU, to averaging the six accuracy benchmarks. v2 also evaluates a Qwen2.5-VL visual-backbone configuration and extends efficiency measurement across lambda settings. Existing dataset splits, training budgets, and individual benchmark metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: The additional backbone experiment tests the framework's portability, while Appendix B.4 adds measured latency and throughput sensitivity to lambda. Existing routing ablations, complementarity analyses, and case studies remain. Appendix B.3 revisits per-dataset routing already examined in Figures 3 and 8 rather than introducing an entirely new analysis question.

E5.justification: Both versions report ten timed runs after five warm-up iterations for path-cost measurement and three differently seeded runs for the 350-sample efficiency benchmark. v2 introduces no new confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests, or repeated-run reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds baseline scores, a Qwen2.5-VL TableDART variant scoring 70.25 average accuracy, and lambda-dependent efficiency results; the primary configuration remains at 74.86. Table 4 corrects InfoTabs from 73.59 to 76.22. Table 5's revised aggregation makes lambda = 0.05 highest at 75.05, without changing individual benchmark scores. New Figure 10 reports routing percentages that disagree with retained Figures 3 and 8.

T1.justification: Equations 1–8, the processing-cost definition, and Algorithm 1's Heuristic Alignment Score are retained. Explicit binary-score notation and the explanation of forward KL restate existing mathematics; no new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation appears.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution list, and conclusion retain the claims of efficient dynamic routing, frozen-backbone modularity, Fusion-based integration, and strong seven-benchmark performance. The headline 4.02-point average accuracy advantage is unchanged. Additional backbone evidence supports the existing generality claim.

C2.justification: Section 4.5 now justifies lambda = 0.15 as an accuracy–latency compromise rather than the best average performer, citing a 0.19-point accuracy sacrifice for 8.4% lower latency. v2 also expands interpretations linking routing to modality strengths and task difficulty. Appendix B.2 nevertheless retains its earlier global-optimum language.

D1.justification: Appendix A.5.2 newly identifies which baseline scores were borrowed from publications and which came from the authors' runs. The reproducibility statement replaces the anonymous repository address with a named GitHub repository and identifies the Bunya computing facility. Existing hardware specifications, hyperparameters, and training-time disclosures remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds literature on TabPedia, SynTab-LLaVA, Qwen2.5-VL, sentence embeddings, and other contextual work. Appendix A.3.2 explicitly relates its standard gate to GShard, Uni-Perceiver, and dynamic multimodal fusion. These additions broaden attribution without substantially changing the positioning against static multimodal processing.

P1.justification: Localized rewrites clarify encoding, target construction, inference, and efficiency interpretation. v2 adds Appendices B.3–B.4, acknowledgments, equal-contribution notation, and the ICLR publication header. The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact.

P2.justification: Table 1 is expanded and rescaled for additional model rows, and Table 5 changes its aggregate label and highlighting. v2 adds routing-distribution Figure 10, accuracy–latency Figure 11, and efficiency Table 11. Existing figures and tables are largely retained with pagination and placement changes.

improvement.justification: v2 adds useful comparisons, baseline-source disclosure, corrected accuracy averaging, and measured efficiency trade-offs. However, new Figure 10 conflicts with retained Figures 3 and 8 for lambda = 0.15. Section 4.3 also interprets the overall TAT-QA Fusion share of 88.7% as a rate among hard cases, which Figure 10 does not establish. These unresolved problems affect the central routing explanation, making the net quality effect uncertain despite clear reporting improvements.
